Supported Housing/Hostels Applicants in supported living or hostels participating in the hostel move-on scheme will be allocated properties in accordance with that scheme (Appendix A) Assessments for applicants who are members of staff or elected members of the council Applications from elected members or members of their family will be dealt with by the Housing Options manager. The award of a priority band and/or an allocation to elected members or to members of their family will need to be authorised by the Chief Executive Officer. Applications from staff members will be dealt with by the Housing Options manager. The award of a priority banding and /or an allocation to staff members will need to be authorised by the council’s Director with responsibility for housing. Determination of application date All applications will be awarded an ‘effective date’ by the council. This is usually the date on which the Home Options application was made. The date will determine who is successful in being offered a property where two or more people from the same band bid on the same property. Change in circumstances If an applicant’s circumstances change it is their responsibility to inform the council so that their application can be reassessed. Examples of a change of circumstances could include the serious deterioration in a medical condition, threat of homelessness or an increase in household size due to the birth of a child. Following the reassessment, if the applicant moves into a higher band their effective date will be the date that the council was notified of, or provided with evidence of, their change of circumstances. Alternatively, if an applicant moves into a lower band then the effective date will revert to the original date they applied for Home Options. It is the applicant’s responsibility to ensure that their contact details are kept up to date. Revision of applications Every Home Options applicant is sent a revision form on the anniversary of their application to ensure that their circumstances are kept up to date. They are required to update, sign and return the form to confirm they wish to remain on the housing register. The Home Options application will automatically be cancelled if the form is not returned. Property size qualification Each applicant will be assessed by the council, to determine what size of property they qualify for. It is expected that participating landlords will seek to maximise occupation of available properties. A general guide showing property size qualification for different household sizes is set out in a table at Appendix E however, each participating landlord may choose to take account of local issues in determining what household size is eligible to bid for a property. This will be made clear at point of advertisement. Any potential affordability or housing benefit issues arising from this will be discussed with the applicant prior to their accepting the tenancy. Notification of applications Once a Home Options application has been assessed the applicant will receive notification from the council confirming the band in which they have been placed. Cancellation of applications Applications will be cancelled by the council for the following reasons: The applicant requests cancellation The applicant's circumstances change and they are no longer eligible The applicant's circumstances change and they no longer qualify The applicant fails to return a revision form The applicant is found to have made a false or deliberately misleading statement in connection with their application The applicant moves outside the Norwich boundary. The applicant has refused offers or failed to attend viewings on three occasions, where no other restrictions apply. Refusals or failure to attend viewings Where no other restrictions apply to the award of banding and an applicant has bid for three properties, which they have refused or where they have failed to attend the viewing without good cause, then their circumstances and banding will be reviewed. If these refusals are considered by a Housing Options team leader or manager to be unreasonable or without grounds, then the Home Options application will be cancelled and no new application will be accepted for a minimum twelve-month period. Misrepresentation or withholding of information It is a criminal offence for anyone to try and obtain accommodation from the council by knowingly giving a false statement or withholding information. If we suspect that an applicant has given false information or withheld information, we will investigate. The Home Options application will be suspended while the investigation is carried out. Failure by an applicant, or someone acting at their instigation, to inform the council of changes to their application, contrivance of circumstances or the deliberate withholding, or misrepresentation of information relevant to their housing circumstances, will mean that the applicant will not to qualify for Home Options and their application will be cancelled for an indefinite period and can be reviewed only after a minimum twelve- month period. Any such action may also result in criminal prosecution. If found guilty the applicant could be liable to a fine and/or imprisonment. The scheme landlord may seek possession of a tenancy that was granted as a result of a false statement and may also attempt to recover any costs incurred. Accessing the housing options Finding a home Once applicants are registered on Home Options they can start looking for a social housing property of their choice. Advertising of vacant properties Properties will be advertised on a weekly basis. Properties will be advertised in two main categories. These will be: For all applicants. For existing (transfer) tenants of the council and scheme landlords only. By these means the council will seek to ensure that at least 20% of allocations made through Home Options are to existing tenants. Properties will be advertised in the following ways: In a newsletter At the council’s website The Home Options bidding cycle runs for the seven days from Wednesday midnight each week. Promotion of other housing options Information will also be provided about the other housing options we will be promoting through the scheme including: Help to stay in your current home (Disabled Facilities Grants, dementia grants and other discretionary loans etc.) Rent Deposit Schemes LetNCC scheme Discretionary Housing Payments Mutual exchanges Help to access properties for shared ownership Property descriptions Properties advertised will, wherever possible, carry a photograph of the property or similar and will have a description of the property. This description will usually include the following information: The type of property (house, flat etc.) The tenure of the property (social rented housing, affordable rent, shared ownership etc.) The number of bedrooms the property has The location of the property The level of accessibility the property has for people with mobility problems/wheelchair users Any services provided to the property e.g. wardens, caretaker etc. The heating type the property has Any age restrictions on the property (sheltered etc.) Whether pets are allowed Availability of outside space (garden etc.) The rent of the property and the service charges. Social rented properties can sometimes have two different rent levels of ‘social rent’ and ‘affordable rent’ and each landlord has their own criteria for which rent level applies to which type of property. This should be clearly explained on each advert, where this is relevant. Special information (location of bus routes/ other amenities etc.) Whether the property is available to all applicants or transfer applicants only Applicants must qualify for the size of property as advertised. The landlord will ascribe tenancy type(s) for their advertised properties. Bidding/application process Provided the applicant meets the stated qualifying criteria they can bid for the property by the deadline given. Deadlines for bids Bidding closes at midnight every Wednesday. Bids received after the specified deadline will not be considered unless there are extenuating circumstances. Any such retrospective bids must be agreed by the Housing Options manager and a record kept of the reasons for acceptance of the retrospective bid held on record for audit purposes. Bidding methods Applicants can bid in the following ways: On the website, www.norwichhomeoptions.org.uk Over the telephone to the Home Options team. Disqualified bids Applicants are restricted to making two bids for social rented properties per week. Applicants will not be considered for any property for which they do not meet the qualifying criteria. For example, a single person would not be considered for a three-bedroom property. Where an applicant who has been awarded a priority banding to reflect a specific housing need has bid for a property which does not meet this housing need, their bid will not be considered. For example, an applicant in a priority band based on a medical need for a ground floor property will not be considered if they have bid for a house or upper floor flat. Selection of the successful bids At the end of the advertising cycle a shortlist will be drawn up from all applicants that have applied for a property. At this point the banding and qualification of any shortlisted applicant will be reviewed for accuracy. The offer of accommodation will be made to the person in the highest band that meets the qualifying criteria. If there is more than one applicant in the band, the offer will be made to any UK armed forces veteran within that band, followed by the applicant who has been waiting the longest within that band. If the applicant with the highest priority refuses the property it will be offered to the next highest bidder and so on. In order to maximise use of adapted properties, where a property has had adaptations to improve accessibility, the scheme landlord has the right to allocate the property to the applicant that has bid who is in greatest need of those specific adaptations at that property. As such, an occupational therapist may be invited to viewings of adapted properties to advise on suitability. A risk and support needs assessment may be carried out. As a result, restrictions may be placed on the area or property which the applicant will be considered for. Applicants will not be offered a property where a risk to themselves or others has been identified. Making the offer The successful applicant will be contacted by the landlord whose property they have applied for to arrange an accompanied viewing. More than one applicant may be invited to the viewing. Photographic identification from the applicant will be required at the viewing. Applicants will usually be contacted within three working days of the advert for the property closing. If an applicant cannot be contacted following multiple attempts the next person on the shortlist will be contacted. It is therefore important that all applicants ensure they are contactable or else they may lose out on a property they have applied for. Applicants have 48 hours to decide whether to accept the offer of accommodation. If no response has been received after this time, the next person on the shortlist will be offered the property. If an applicant refuses the offer, the property will be offered to the next on the shortlist, and so on until the property is let. Scheme landlords reserve the right to carry out an assessment on applicants to ensure the particular property is appropriate. If the landlord deems the property not to be suitable for the applicant, the property would then be offered to the next applicant on the shortlist. Offers of accommodation may be withdrawn if it is found that the information supplied by the applicant was incorrect or if they are deemed due to their behaviour to not qualify (e.g. if they have accrued rent arrears that were not previously known about). Hostel move-on The Norwich hostel move on agreement (appendix D) sets out how applicants in participant hostels and supported accommodation who meet the criteria will be allocated social housing. Properties excluded from the scheme The council reserves the right to exclude certain properties and housing schemes from the allocations system. Examples of where this may occur are: Where a property is needed urgently to deal with an emergency. Specialist housing schemes, for example Housing with Care Schemes will also be let outside the allocations scheme. Direct lets In certain circumstances the council will allocate properties directly to applicants, outside of the usual process. Illustrative examples of direct lets are as follows: Where an allocation is required to ensure protection of the public, for example, following a decision made by a Multi-Agency Public Protection Panel meeting, or where an applicant has been referred as part of the witness protection scheme. Where the council or a scheme landlord has entered a special arrangement with a support agency in order to accommodate especially vulnerable or challenging clients. Any such arrangement will be governed by an agreement signed off by the Head of Housing. Where the tenant of a scheme landlord’s home is being repaired and is not occupiable so that they need to be moved from the property on a temporary or permanent basis. Where a client has been accepted as statutorily homeless, they will be direct let the first suitable available property. As part of the council’s ‘hostel move-on’ scheme (see Appendix D) A tenancy may also be allocated by the council or scheme landlord, regardless of other priorities, where the applicant has enjoyed established occupancy of the property, has a reasonable expectation of a property of that type and would be a suitable tenant, (e.g. non-secure tenants, or carers or family members with no succession rights.) In deciding whether to make an offer of a tenancy the landlord will consider whether the property is of a suitable size and type for the applicant’s household and the conduct of the applicant in terms of rent arrears and tenancy conditions. Decisions to allocate properties outside of Home Options will be authorised by the Housing Options manager and held on record. Sensitive lets Sensitive lets are used where a specific issue has been identified in a particular area or block, making a property unsuitable for allocation to some applicants. When considering a sensitive let, instead of allocating a property to the applicant at the top of the list, the landlord will consider the suitability of each applicant who has bid for the vacancy. This will be based on information held about the applicant and on knowledge of the property, its location or neighbours. The council will only use sensitive lets in exceptional circumstances. In order to ensure that all decisions on sensitive lets are accountable, transparent and monitored, all decisions must be agreed by the Housing Options manager and the respective manager of the scheme landlord and a record held on file. Local lettings plans Local lettings plans are used by landlords to develop policies and letting arrangements that: Respond to local housing need and demand Help to suitably match applicants to properties; and Help them to achieve a balanced housing mix within a particular area. The main aim of a local lettings plan is to build a strong and sustainable community. Local lettings plans are generally used when allocating new build housing for the first time. New build developments are unusual in terms of housing allocations because of the number of properties that are available for let in a short period of time in one area. This makes sure that: new build programmes meet the widest possible range of needs; and the council avoids the creation of groups of vulnerable households in specific communities. To make sure that all decisions on local lettings agreements are accountable, transparent and monitored, all decisions must be agreed by the Housing Options manager and the respective manager of the scheme landlord and a record held on file. Sheltered Housing Sheltered housing is accommodation designed specifically for older people. Residents may pay an additional charge for support services. The minimum age for the landlord to consider an applicant for sheltered housing will be clearly stated when each property is advertised. The council and scheme landlords may carry out a needs and risk assessment for customers who bid for sheltered housing properties, to ensure the services provided are appropriate to their needs. This will be done as part of the offer process. Statement on equal access The council and scheme landlords are committed to ensuring equality of opportunity in all elements of the scheme. This means that we seek to ensure that priority for housing is based on housing need and that housing policies are fair to all sections of the community regardless of age, disability, gender, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, or sexual orientation. We want our services to be accessible to everyone who lives in Norwich. If you need extra help to be able to use our services, such as translation and interpretation services, large print or signing, please tell us. All applicants for housing or rehousing may be asked to provide details of age, disability, gender, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, or sexual orientation. This is to allow us to assess the application properly as well as to monitor who is allocated housing, and to ensure that properties are being offered and allocated fairly. Advice and assistance The council will ensure that everybody in Norwich seeking housing can easily access the information and assistance they require to use the scheme effectively and we will provide advice on the range of housing options open to them. Staff will be available throughout office hours to provide advice and assistance on the full range of housing options available. Vulnerable groups Due to the nature of Home Options, particularly the need for applicants to be proactive in the process, the council realises it is essential that vulnerable and excluded people can participate effectively. The council will therefore ensure all relevant staff are well trained so that they can assist vulnerable applicants to access and use the scheme. All literature will be available in a large font and written in plain and unambiguous language. The website is compatible with screen readers and has browse aloud capability. The council will also hold an ‘assisted applicants list’ for those who, due to their vulnerability, require additional help with the scheme. This additional help includes helping applicants bid for available homes or sending the property brochures directly to people who cannot access the internet. The ‘assisted applicants list’ can be accessed by applicants or their support workers informing the council. This service will only be available for the most vulnerable clients as determined by the council. To ensure vulnerable groups are not being disadvantaged under the scheme, the council will monitor systems to ensure all groups are using the scheme successfully. Reviews of decisions Notifying an ineligible or non-qualifying applicant: The council will notify an applicant in writing of any decision that they: Are ineligible for Home Options Do not qualify to join Home Options. In each instance, the council will give clear grounds for the decision. An applicant can ask for a review of certain decisions made regarding Home Options. These are: That they are not eligible or do not qualify Their band and effective date The type of property that they can bid/apply for A request for a review of a decision must be made in writing within 21 days of receipt of the decision. The decision will be reviewed by a Housing Options team leader or manager or, in complex cases, an assessment panel. The role of the reviewer is to ensure that policy has been correctly applied. We aim to complete all review and medical assessments within 56 days of the request but in some circumstances this timeframe may be extended. The applicant will be notified in writing of the decision. In requesting a review of their qualification for Home Options, the applicant will normally be expected to show that they have addressed issues which caused them not to qualify for the scheme over a minimum 12-month period, clearly demonstrating to the council’s satisfaction that their behaviour has been addressed and they are able to independently maintain a tenancy. The applicant’s individual circumstances will be fully considered as part of any review and each case will be treated on its merits. Where an applicant does not qualify for Home Options through rent arrears, the council has set out in Appendix B the repayment arrangements and timeframes expected to be maintained in order for the applicant to demonstrate that the issue is being satisfactorily addressed. An applicant does not have the right to ask for a further review. Complaints procedure If an applicant is dissatisfied with any aspect of the management of their Home Options application, other than where a review can be made, they should follow the council’s complaints procedure, details of which can be found at the website www.norwich.gov.uk. The council will not accept a complaint for issues where there is or has already been a right of appeal, for example reviews of Home Options banding or qualification. Local Government & Social Care Ombudsman If a complainant is not satisfied with the action the council takes, he or she can send a written complaint to the ombudsman. A complainant must give the organisation an opportunity to deal with a complaint first, using its complaints procedure. The Local Government & Social Care Ombudsman can be contacted at: Tel: 0300 061 0614. Website: www.lgo.org.uk Confidentiality statement Norwich City Council is committed to protecting the rights of privacy and processing will be conducted fairly, lawfully and transparently in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (EU 2016/679) and all other applicable data protection law (‘Data protection legislation’). We will ensure the personal information of all applicants (new, existing and former) is: Stored lawfully Processed in a fair and transparent manner Collected for a specific, explicit and legitimate purpose The data will be kept up to date and held until it is no longer required Shared only with other organisations for legitimate processing, the prevention of fraud or with the person’s explicit consent. Our Privacy Notice can be located online at: www.norwich.gov.uk When an application is made to Home Options, the applicant will be asked to give permission for information to be obtained from, or shared with, third parties, which would be required to enable the Home Options assessment or an allocation of housing to proceed. If an applicant bids on a property advertised on Home Options, their data will be shared with the council or housing association that owns the property to enable the accurate and fair matching of people to properties to take place. Home Options partners and housing associations may also make enquires with council housing benefit departments and other agencies such as medical practitioners, DWP, support agencies, police and landlords to confirm the details provided by applicants. Monitoring/changes to the scheme Scheme monitoring The scheme will be monitored directly by the Housing Options manager. The manager will, where necessary make recommendations for changes to the scheme, taking into consideration the following: Application and bidding data, property turnover and demand That the highest needs applicants and those who are vulnerable are using the scheme effectively The scheme’s performance in meeting its agreed aims Feedback from applicants and stakeholders That the scheme continues to address local housing issues. Changes to the scheme The council reserves the right to expand, change or alter any element of the scheme, as and when required, to meet changes in housing need, capacity, resources and legislation. Any major changes to the scheme will be carried out through a report of the Housing Options Manager to the council executive, following consultation with scheme landlords. Appendices Appendix A Scheme Landlords Broadland Housing Association Orwell Housing Association Cotman Housing Association Orbit East Housing Association Guinness Trust Flagship Peddars Way Housing Association Wherry Housing Association Saffron Housing Trust Hastoe Housing Association Places for People Housing Association Habinteg Housing Association Granta Housing Society Victory Housing Trust Norwich City Council Suffolk Housing Association Appendix B Guideline repayment arrangements and timelines Where an applicant does not qualify through rent arrears alone and is seeking a review of the decision, the guideline repayment arrangements and timeframes expected to be maintained in order for the applicant to demonstrate that they are suitable to be a tenant are set out as follows: Applicants with a cumulative debt outstanding of £500 - £700 are likely to be ineligible unless they have a repayment plan in place and adhered to for a minimum of six months, or the rent account is cleared, whichever is sooner. If the debts relate to a former tenancy it is expected that the applicant can evidence a minimum six months settled accommodation with an up to date rent account and no tenancy issues. Applicants with a cumulative debt outstanding of over £1000 are likely to be ineligible unless they have a repayment plan in place and adhered to for a minimum of twelve months or the rent account is cleared, whichever is sooner. If the debts relate to a former tenancy it is expected that the applicant can evidence a minimum twelve months settled accommodation with up to date rent account and no tenancy issues. Where the council assesses that, in the cases above, that an applicant becomes eligible for Home Options, a reduced preference will apply for so long as the debt exists. Where an applicant does not qualify through their behaviour and is seeking a review of the decision, they are expected to be able to evidence that they have successfully addressed the issue which caused them not to qualify through successfully maintaining an independent tenancy, without on-site support, for an appropriate period of time and there have been no recurrences of that behaviour or any other which would affect their ability to manage a tenancy. In such instances the appropriate period of time will relate to the severity of the issue and will be confirmed to the applicant at the point they are advised that they do not qualify. Exceptional circumstances will be taken into account and the applicant’s individual circumstances will be fully considered and the case treated on its own merits. Appendix C LetNCC tenancy incentives scheme LetNCC is the council’s private sector leasing scheme, designed to use privately leased and managed accommodation to house clients who are facing homelessness. LetNCC accommodation is, by its nature, not permanent. Therefore, the LetNCC tenancy incentive scheme is designed to ensure a pathway for clients through LetNCC accommodation and into a secure tenancy via Home Options. Priority banding can only be awarded upon written submission by the LetNCC team, with the referral to be agreed by the LetNCC team-leader and the decision to be made by a review panel. Successful referrals, as agreed by the review panel, will be prioritised as follows: Gold band Families who have been LetNCC tenants for at least two years where the tenancy has been well managed, there have been no rent arrears or debts to the council and no matters of concern. Silver band Single clients and couples who have been LetNCC tenants for at least two years where the tenancy has been well managed, there have been no rent arrears or debts to the council and no matters of concern. Clients that meet the Home Options qualifying criteria but have not been referred or do not meet the criteria for higher banding under the tenancy incentive scheme will be placed in the low need band, notwithstanding any other issues which may affect their banding in accordance with policy. Appendix D Norwich Hostel Move-on Agreement 2025 1. The agreement This agreement is made between: Norwich City Council YMCA Norfolk St Martins Housing Trust Sanctuary Supported Living Hinde House (Orwell Housing Association) Hope into Action Stonham Home Group (herein referred to as "the parties") The parties wish to co-operate in order to establish and maintain a hostel move-on scheme. The parties have agreed to enter into this agreement to record their respective intentions. The purpose of the scheme is to provide a co-ordinated route into and out of hostel and supported accommodation services in Norwich. The parties agree as follows: 2. Objectives The agreed objectives are as follows: To reduce rough sleeping and homelessness in Norwich. To operate the scheme so that those in greatest need can access hostel accommodation quickly and easily. To provide a co-ordinated hostel system in Norwich which makes best use of its resources. To enable clients to move through different stages of supported accommodation to best meet their needs. The parties will need to create robust move on plans to support internal moves. To ensure all hostel clients can move on with the appropriate support to ensure sustainability. Comply with attendance at the monthly Norwich Accommodation Meetings. The parties agree to co-operate fully with each other for the achievement of these objectives. 3. The process Nominations arrangements: An initial assessment of the client’s needs, and potential accommodation outcomes will be considered by the parties as part of the referral process and will be ongoing. Issues such as social care needs, local connection and potential for move-on will be considered as part of the assessment. Where agreed, clients can be moved between providers to prevent eviction or whether alternative provision is deemed more appropriate. Following assessment, homeless and individuals sleeping rough will be referred into accommodation appropriate to their needs. Clients can be moved between provision where it is agreed by the Norwich Accommodation Meeting and the providers. Individual services retain the right the refuse a referral should they deem the risk too high. Vacancies created by successful move-on will be discussed at the Norwich Accommodation Meeting, with a focus on optimising bed-spaces. Move-on process for hostel residents Applicants in supported housing/hostels who participate in the Norwich hostel move on agreement who are assessed as needing to move on as determined by a member of the Housing Options team will be direct let into appropriate social housing tenancy providing the following criteria is met. Local connection and reconnection Norwich City Council is committed to providing the best possible service to all homeless people, including single homeless people not in priority need. Unfortunately, social housing and supported housing is a scarce resource and we need to ensure that services are prioritised for people with a local connection to Norwich City Council area. It needs to be recognised that people that have lived in Norwich their whole lives may only have a connection to Norwich, whilst newly arrived people sleeping rough to the area are likely to have other options available to them in the area that they are connected to. Clients will need to be evidenced as having lived in Norwich for at least two years, including for six months before their referral into the participating hostel or supported accommodation. Individuals who have been sleeping rough for six months within this period will not be considered eligible for a direct offer of social housing. Clients that do not meet this criteria will not qualify and will be expected to explore alternative housing options or reconnection to their home area with support from the hostel provider. Risk The current support provider will provide a risk assessment. Qualification will be determined by a Housing Options officer using criteria set out in Home Options policy in regard unacceptable behaviour and qualification will be applied. Tenancy ready The client must be able to demonstrate that they are able to maintain a tenancy, for example, but not limited to, through an approved tenancy awareness course so that it is reasonable to expect that any tenancy will be sustained. Previous issues such as rent arrears, or anti-social behaviour will be evidenced as having been addressed. Personalise housing plan The applicant will complete a personalised housing plan (PHP) with a Home Options officer. Any special housing requirements will be agreed and set out in this document. Applicants demonstrating the above will receive one offer of accommodation via a direct let, which they are expected to accept. If the client refuses the offer, they will be removed from the process and cannot reapply for move-on through the scheme. The client has the right to request a review of the offer of accommodation on the grounds of suitability. This will be carried out by a review panel in accordance with Home Options policy. Those who do not qualify for move-on Any individual has the right to apply to join the Home Options scheme and not be subject to restrictions that the move-on process imposes. The application will be assessed on the qualification criteria set out in Home Options policy. Clients in hostels or supported accommodation will be assessed as adequately housed and therefore placed in the standard band. Where the client is assessed by the provider as ready to move-on and this has been agreed by the Home Options team but does not qualify for the move-on process, their Home Options application will be placed in the bronze band. Given the extremely high levels of demand for social housing in Norwich, clients that do not meet the criteria for move-on will be encouraged to be realistic in their expectations and be supported by their support provider to seek alternative options such as house-share, privately renting and reconnection to their home area. If a hostel client in bronze band refuses a reasonable offer of accommodation, this will result in their Home Options application being placed in the standard band. 4. Compliance monitoring If Norwich City Council deems that the provider is not meeting the terms set out in this agreement, they hold the right to temporarily suspend the party from the Move on agreement for 3 months or terminate the agreement with that provider altogether. All hostel providers (The Parties) agree to compliance monitoring by Norwich City Council and agree to submit reports every two months to evidence the following: Terms of compliance The referral source to evidence keeping within nomination agreement. Evidence of housing history and former rough sleeping ** Full breakdown of all Move On outcomes Area of Local connection at the point of access to the hostel Support needs Attendance at Norwich Accommodation Meeting and Hostel Forum away days Submission of thoroughly reviewed Move on Paperwork with sign off by management. This ensures high standards and helps prevent delays due to ongoing communication between NCC and hostel providers. NCC can provide a training guide as a reference. 5. The role of Norwich Accommodation Meeting (NAM) The Norwich Accommodation Meeting takes place in person, on a monthly basis with representatives of each of the parties and outreach services. It is expected that each representative is able to make operational decisions on behalf of their respective organisation. In addition to the activities set out above, the Norwich Accommodation meeting will: Discuss clients who have been evicted from hostels in the last 4 weeks (The agreement is also that Providers are informing Norwich City Council of evictions where possible before they take place and where not possible beforehand, notices of immediate evictions. Make decisions on current vacancies and share information with other hostel providers. Where required, the meeting will make decisions on moves between providers and explore the moving of clients from one provider to another to prevent eviction and abandonments. Discuss clients who are threatened with eviction from hostels and supported accommodation and explore ways this can be prevented. Where appropriate, discuss current individuals that are rough sleeping and their potential accommodation solutions within the hostel system. Discuss clients ready for move-on into social housing through Home Options and any issues affecting this. Monitor the efficacy of this scheme. In addition to the Norwich Accommodation Meetings providers are asked to commit to attendance the Norwich Hostel Forum that takes place every 4 months. The purpose of the hostel forum away days are to, but not limited to: To share what works well / Shared best practice. Pool training where applicable. Feedback outcomes / observations to the existing Greater Norwich Homelessness partnership. To propose changes to the Move On / Hostel system which would improve performance. 6. Practicalities Term of the agreement The agreement will be reviewed after two years. Should the parties wish to extend the term, this will be done by variation to this agreement three months prior to the end of term and with the agreement of the parties. Sharing and handling of information The parties shall ensure that they and their employees observe all their obligations under General Data Protection Regulation which arise in connection with this agreement. Prior to the issue of any press release or making any contact with the press on any matter relating to the agreement the parties shall consult with each other, initially through the Norwich Accommodation Meeting. Confidentiality Each party shall keep the other’s information confidential unless: The information was already lawfully known. Disclosure or use of the information is necessary to meet the terms of this agreement. Disclosure is required by law (including under the Freedom of Information Act 2000) or disclosure is permitted by the Human Rights Act 1998. Variation No amendment to or variation of this agreement shall take effect unless it is agreed by the parties in writing and signed by an authorised representative of each of the parties. Termination A party may only terminate this agreement by giving the other parties three months’ written notice. Complaints and disputes resolution Complaints in relation to the performance, success or otherwise of this agreement shall be passed, in the first instance, to the Housing Options manager at Norwich City Council who will try and resolve them with the relevant parties. Where resolution is not reached, the issue will be escalated to the directors of the involved services. Appendix E Download the guide showing property size qualification for different household sizes. documents.title: Allocations Policy 2025 – Briefing Note
documents.text: Norwich Home Options Allocation Policy 2025/2026 – Briefing Note-Norwich Home Options Allocation Policy 2025/2026 – Briefing Note- Norwich Home Options Allocation Policy 2025/2026 – Briefing Note - Norwich Home Options Allocation Policy 2025/2026 – Briefing Note - Briefing Note: Home Options policy changes 2025/2026 Part VI of the Housing Act determines that local authorities must have an allocation scheme to determine priorities between applicants for social housing and to set out the procedure to be followed when allocating social housing in their area. In Norwich, the allocation scheme is called Home Options. The current Home Options allocations policy dates from October 2021 and needs updating to incorporate new legislation and statutory guidance. The update also presents the opportunity to ensure that policy reflects local needs and issues. Key proposed changes Norwich is a ‘flow’ city; the centre of a large rural area which attracts inward migration for reasons such as employment, housing and education. In accordance with government guidelines, and to ensure that the council’s housing policies benefit long term local residents, Home Options applicants must have been continuously resident in Norwich for the last two years (currently six months) in order to qualify. For household members to join an application and to be included in any assessment of housing need, the same criteria apply. Exceptions, as set down in legislation, will apply. Other authorities in a similar position have recently extended their local connection criteria, as have other Norfolk local authorities. The council has several strategies in place to mitigate the adverse effects of this increase in continuous residency requirements on those most likely to be affected by the change: Norwich City Council has formed a specialist refugee housing advice team that uses targeted grants to help individuals leaving asylum-seeker accommodation access housing in the private rental sector. For prison leavers, the council has a specialist housing advice team which uses government funding to facilitate access to the private rented sector, thereby reducing homelessness and re-offending. To focus limited resources more effectively, the number of property refusals allowed before an application is reviewed and may be cancelled for 12 months will be reduced from five to three to reflect extremely high demand. This will not apply to homelessness clients, who, as per legislation, receive one offer. In accordance with the Armed Forces Covenant, on property shortlisting, where there is more than one applicant in the band, the offer will be made to any UK armed forces veteran within that band, followed by the applicant who has been waiting the longest within that band. If the applicant with the highest priority refuses the property it will be offered to the next highest bidder and so on. Minor proposed changes Clarification: All applications will involve a discussion of an applicant’s housing need with an adviser. Applicants who do not meet the criteria for a priority banding category are extremely unlikely to be rehoused through the Home Options scheme and will be given advice about alternative housing options. Clarification: The council will not consider the following as members of an applicant’s household: Relatives who do not form part of the applicant’s immediate family where there is no formal care arrangement; parents or step-parents, grandparents, brothers or step-brothers, sisters or step-sisters, aunts, uncles, grandchildren, nieces, nephews, cousins. Clarification Residents in prison, bail hostel, hospital or approved premises, or those households referred into or placed into any form of accommodation in Norwich by another local authority will not gain a local connection. Clarification: Silver band for rough sleeping will be applied where it has been confirmed that an applicant is sleeping rough, meets the qualification criteria and it has been assessed that there is no other accommodation available to them. The council will verify that an applicant is sleeping rough before awarding this priority and banding will be subject to ongoing, regular verification and support to explore off the street accommodation options. Rough sleeping priority will not be awarded when the client does not engage with the council’s support or where accommodation has been made available to the applicant, including a placement at a direct access hostel, supported accommodation or in the private rented sector, but the applicant chooses not to take up this offer of accommodation. Any banding determination will be made in conjunction with the council’s rough sleeping team. Applicants assessed as ‘sleeping rough’ will not be awarded additional priority on any other accommodation related factors. Clarification: For the award of homelessness and prevention priority, applicants will have completed and kept to a personalised housing plan made with a housing adviser, will place or have placed for them two bids per week with the guidance of their adviser and will be entitled to one suitable offer of accommodation Clarification: Deliberate worsening of circumstances (standard band) will be applied to those who unreasonably fail to follow advice given by the council in order to prevent homelessness. Clarification: Welfare priority: In some instances, the assessment panel may award priority banding on a time limited basis and/or apply conditions to bidding. documents.title: Allocations Policy 2025 – Equality Impact Assessment
documents.text: Equality Impact Assessment What is being assessed Norwich Home Options Allocation Policy Status Assessment of a statutory function update Officer completing this form Graduate Management Trainee Team Home Options Directorate Communities and Housing SLT sponsor Executive director of communities and housing Date assessment commenced 28th October 2025 Date of completion 4th November 2025 Will the report this EqIA relates to go to Committee? Scrutiny Committee (15th January 2025) What are the main aims or purpose of the strategy, policy, plan, project, contract or major change to your service which you are considering? Part 4 of the Housing Act determines that local authorities must have an allocation scheme to determine priorities between applicants for Norwich City Council owned (social) housing and to set out the procedure to be followed when allocating social housing in their area. In Norwich, the allocation scheme is called Home Options. The current Home Options allocations policy dates from October 2021 and needs updating to incorporate new legislation and statutory guidance. The update also presents the opportunity to ensure that policy reflects local needs and issues. This EqIA covers the entire policy, highlighting specific proposed changes to the policy: (a) local connection requirement increased from 6 months to 2 years (b) reduction in permitted social housing refusals from 5 to 3 (c) prioritisation of armed forces veterans on housing shortlists within each band How does it fit with other services and policies, and how does it support our corporate priorities? Revisions to the Housing Allocations policy were developed in parallel with the development of the Norwich Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy (2025–2030). These policy changes are closely aligned with the strategy and support the operational work of the homelessness prevention and relief teams. The revised housing register eligibility and prioritisation criteria will promote social housing allocation to the most vulnerable local people who are engaged with home options, including those at risk of homelessness or who are currently homeless. These policy revisions will influence both who can join the register and how quickly they may be allocated housing. The new housing allocation policy aligns to the “A Fairer Norwich” community-led plan priority: working to support local people and families so that they can face economic and social challenges. The policy aims to reduce inequality and the negative effects of poverty by prioritising social housing allocation for those who are the most in need within our city. What is the reason for the proposal or change (financial, legal etc)? The council has a statutory requirement to review and update their housing allocations policy in line with any significant changes to legislation, local priorities or local needs. In line with the update of the Homelessness and Rough Sleeping strategy (2025-2030), the allocations policy was reviewed and updated. Who will be affected by this strategy, policy, plan, project, contract or major change to your service? (Please tick all that apply) ☒ Residents ☐ Visitors ☐ Council Staff ☐ Businesses ☐ Workers Please state any specific client group or groups Specific groups impacted by this policy are: Norwich City Council social housing tenants Individuals applying for Norwich City Council home options Individuals at risk of homelessness Individuals experiencing homelessness Which wards will be impacted by your proposal? Does your proposal impact any of the council’s Reducing Inequality Target Areas (RITAs)? ☒ ALL Norwich City Council wards ☐ Bowthorpe ☐ Catton Grove ☐ Crome ☐ Eaton ☐ Lakenham ☐ Mancroft ☐ Mile Cross ☐ Nelson ☐ Sewell ☐ Thorpe Hamlet ☐ Town Close ☐ University ☐ Wensum ☒ Catton Grove☒ North City Centre ☒ Earlham ☒ Pilling Park ☒ Heartsease☒ Vauxhall Street ☒ Mid Lakenham ☒ West Pottergate and Russell Street ☒ Mile Cross What outcomes do you want to achieve, why and for who? Norwich has experienced significant population growth over the last decade and is the most densely populated district in Norfolk. Norwich, as with any city, faces some challenges including significant and entrenched inequality and deprivation: the latest data published by the End Child Poverty Coalition shows that between 2023-2024, 35.3% of children in Norwich were living in households below the poverty line. As of October 2025, Norwich City Council owns a total of 14,211 properties, which includes 13,291 general needs homes and 920 sheltered homes. Despite this stock, the 2021 Greater Norwich Housing Needs Assessment projected a significant shortfall in social housing provision. Demand continues to outpace supply, particularly among Home Options applicants who are unable to access the increasingly unaffordable private rental sector. The need for appropriate housing for vulnerable individuals and families is both urgent and well-evidenced. Homelessness is associated with significant health consequences for all experiencing it, including mental illness, infectious disease, heart disease, and early mortality (Crisis UK). Young people experiencing housing instability are more likely to be absent or excluded from school, while parents face heightened risks of depression and anxiety due to housing insecurity (Local Government Association, 2017). Older adults, particularly those over 60, are at increased risk of developing depression and dementia (Local Government Association, 2017). Temporary accommodation (TA) exacerbates these issues: two-thirds of TA residents report its negative impact on their mental and physical health (Shelter, 2023), and children residing in temporary housing for over a year are three times as likely to experience anxiety, depression, and infection compared to their housed peers (Shelter, 2006). Once within the social housing system, household changes can lead to overcrowding; a lack of available, larger homes prevents households from moving, thereby increasing their likelihood of mental illness, sleep disturbance, second-hand tobacco exposure, relationship breakdown, and poor educational attainment for children (WHO, 2018). A lack of stable housing additionally negatively impacts job and educational attainment, perpetuating the factors that entrap individuals in poverty and increase their need for social housing provision to prevent their homelessness (Crisis UK). Certain groups are disproportionately affected by homelessness risk or its negative consequences, including families with children, those who are pregnant, army veterans, care leavers, refugees, those fleeing abuse, those experiencing severe mental illness, and those with complex, multiple needs (St Martin in the Fields UK). To mitigate these harms and prevent homelessness among the most vulnerable through a very limited number of council-owned homes, the Home Options allocation policy must prioritise those in greatest need within Norwich. This prioritisation is primarily guided by statutory and legislative frameworks, supplemented by locally informed criteria that reflect emerging trends and community needs. What evidence and data has been used for this assessment, including community engagement and consultation? The new home options allocation policy will go through numerous stages of consultation and debate before sign-off. The draft policy revisions, alongside its summary report and this EqIA, will be uploaded to Get Talking Norwich for the public to view, to allow engagement and comments from the community. The results of this consultation will be considered before the revised policy is assessed and debated within scrutiny committee. This EqIA will also be revised following public consultation. Amendments and suggestions from scrutiny committee will be implemented as appropriate before the final revised policy will go to the council’s cabinet for sign off. Who implements, carries out or delivers the policy, practice, service or function? The home options, homelessness prevention, and homelessness relief teams. Will anyone be disproportionately affected by what you are proposing, and/or will it create any benefits? Due to additions to revised policy: Populations impacted positively: Armed Forces Veterans Populations with extra support in place to mitigate impact: Refugees Ex-offenders If yes, complete the relevant sections overleaf for any benefits and adverse impacts identified. Affected group Key findings from analysis of data and evidence. Identify any gaps in data here Level & type of impact: Actions to mitigate impacts, maximise benefits or address identified gaps in data By when dd/mm/yy A group defined by age (60+) No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Those with physical access or mobility needs Positive Impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Gold priority banding will be awarded to those in severe medical need who need urgent re-housing due to a strongly evidenced, serious and enduring medical condition or disability, which is severely and permanently affected by their current accommodation. This includes those who are housebound through mobility issues and moving to alternative accommodation would alleviate this, and those who have a terminal illness, where alternative accommodation would allow for suitable care to be provided. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☐ Medium impact ☒ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Ongoing Those that identify as disabled Extra support in place to mitigate impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) People with learning disabilities or neurodivergence may face barriers in navigating the application process or understanding eligibility criteria. ☐ Positive impact ☒ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact Extra support for this group: The council’s Home Options team will continue to support all residents who need help with their housing needs, including those who require information in more accessible formats. We are committed to ensuring that everyone can access housing information in a way that meets their individual communication needs. The Home Options team hold a assisted applicants list for relevant applicants that require further support from the team to ensure they are not disadvantaged by the relative complexity of the Home Options application processes. Ongoing Gender reassignment No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Marriage and civil partnership No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Pregnancy and maternity No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Race/ethnicity No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Religion and belief No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Sex No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Sexual orientation No specific impact identified N/A N/A N/A N/A Socio-economic hardship Positive Impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Norwich has high levels of deprivation, with over a third of children living below the poverty line. Many residents face barriers to accessing private rental housing due to affordability, insecure employment, or benefit restrictions. These groups are disproportionately represented among Home Options applicants. As such, the Home Options team hold an assisted applicants list for relevant applicants that require further support from the team to ensure they are not disadvantaged by the relative complexity of the Home Options application processes. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact Overall, the policy aligns with anti-poverty objectives in the council’s community-led plan. Its prioritisation of applicants in greatest housing need supports those experiencing poverty. Ongoing Refugees and Migrants Extra support in place to mitigate impact on this population: (Due to addition to revised policy: (a) local connection requirement increased from 6 months to 2 years) Many asylum seekers are housed in Norwich-based accommodation while awaiting the outcome of their applications. If granted refugee status, they have 28 days to secure permanent housing. Although their residence in Norwich begins upon placement within asylum accommodation, the refugee-application process typically lasts significantly less than the two years required to qualify for the housing register, limiting their options for permanent accommodation upon exit. ☐ Positive impact ☒ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact Extra support for this group: Norwich City Council has formed a specialist refugee housing team that uses targeted grants to help individuals leaving asylum dispersal accommodation access private rental sector, thereby bypassing the continuous residence requirement for social housing. The council aims to continue to enable the success. provided by the refugee housing specialists. Ongoing Armed Forces (includes those who have served or continue to serve in our Armed Forces) Positive Impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) As Norwich City Council has signed the Armed Forces Covenant, people with particular connections to the military don’t need to meet local connection rules when applying for home options. This includes people currently serving or who have served in the regular Armed Forces; bereaved spouses or civil partners who must leave military housing after their partner dies, if the death was related to their service; former reserve force members with serious health issues caused by their service; and divorced or separated spouses or civil partners who are required to leave Ministry of Defence accommodation. Armed forces members and veterans are at a significantly risk of developing illness because of their service, resulting in their increased vulnerability. As such, gold priority banding will be awarded to Armed Forces members and veterans suffering from mental or physical ill health as a result of their service (where this is strongly evidenced, serious and enduring, and is severely and permanently affected by their current accommodation). (Due to addition to revised policy: (c) prioritisation of Armed Forces veterans on shortlists) UK Armed Forces veterans will also have the highest priority within any band they are placed in. On property shortlisting, where there is more than one applicant in the band, the offer will be made to any UK Armed Forces veteran within that band, followed by the applicant who has been waiting the longest within that band. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☐ Medium impact ☒ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Ongoing. Other groups – Ex Offenders Extra support in place to mitigate impact on this population: (Due to addition to revised policy: local connection requirement increased from 6 months to 2 years) Housing ex-offenders upon their release from prison, alongside providing holistic support services, has been shown to reduce re-offending rates by 50% (Department of Levelling Up, Housing and Communities, 2023). It is important to note, however, that there is insufficient evidence to show that housing alone produces this effect (Ministry of Justice Analytical Series, 2025). Home Options eligibility requirements restrict ex-offenders from accessing social housing in two ways. Under the Home Options allocations policy, individuals detained in Norwich-based prisons, bail hostels, or approved premises do not gain a local connection to the area through residing in these premises. Ex-offenders additionally face exclusion from Home Options based on behaviour-based criteria including histories of anti-social behaviour, domestic violence, and convictions for violent crime. ☐ Positive impact ☒ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact Extra support for this group: A homelessness prevention referral can be made to the council by the probation service 8 weeks before an individual is released from prison, where work can begin to prevent their homelessness upon release. This mitigates the need for the applicant to present to the council themselves. Several housing alternatives are available to ex-offenders, including supported accommodation and private rentals. Norwich City Council has developed a specialist ex-offender housing team that utilises the Accommodation for Ex-Offenders (AfEO) fund (a central government fund that helps local authorities provide stable housing and support for individuals leaving prison, thereby reducing homelessness and connected reoffending rates) to help them secure residence within the private rented sector. Since 2023, 91 ex-offenders have been housed through this approach. AfEO funding will end in April 2026, but the council aims to continue the success provided by the ex-offender housing specialists. Applicants excluded from Home Options if based on behaviour-based criteria may re-gain access if they can demonstrate that they have addressed these issues, as outlined in sections 5.0.4 and 5.0.5 of the policy. Ongoing. Other groups – Care Leavers Positive impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Care leavers aged 18-21 years (or up to 25 years old if they are pursuing a programme of education agreed in their pathway plan) that are assessed as ‘needing to move on’ bypass the local connection requirements and are awarded gold priority banding, subject to criteria. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☐ Medium impact ☒ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Ongoing Other groups – those fleeing domestic abuse Positive impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Policy provides local connection exceptions and gold priority banding when safety needs are verified. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☐ Medium impact ☒ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Ongoing Other groups – those living in overcrowded accommodation Positive impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Gold priority banding will be awarded to applicants lacking two or more bedrooms. Silver priority banding will be awarded to applicants lacking one bedroom and those verified as ‘sofa surfing’. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☐ Medium impact ☒ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Other groups – those at risk of homelessness, those who are homeless, and those who are rough sleeping Positive Impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Where the council has accepted a homelessness prevention or relief duty for an applicant who does not hold a priority need, such applicants will be awarded a silver priority banding, subject to criteria. Applicants who are verified to be sleeping rough will be awarded silver priority banding, subject to criteria. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Other groups – families with young children Positive Impact: (In line with current Home Options Allocation Policy) Applicants with dependent children under the age of 10 who live in a flat or maisonette that does not have its own private outdoor space are awarded silver priority banding. Households that include children aged six or under, who live in a property on the third floor or above where there is no lift access, will move up one further priority band. ☒ Positive impact ☐ Adverse impact ☐ Low impact ☒ Medium impact ☐ High impact N/A – Allocation priority outlined in policy. Are there any negative impacts that cannot reasonably be avoided? Increasing the local connection requirement to two years will impact recent arrivals, refugees, and people placed in prison who return to Norwich. The change is a government guideline-based decision that prioritises limited social housing for long‑term local residents. Targeted mitigations will be provided, such as continued refugee private rental support, ex‑offender private rental support, and exception routes and enhanced priority banding for care leavers, domestic abuse victims and army veterans. How has the equality impact assessment informed or changed the proposal? This EqIA has highlighted the key groups likely to be affected by the policy and reinforced the need for the continuation of the services which work to mitigate these impacts. These include the specialist rental support teams for refugees and ex-offenders. What actions have been identified going forward? Moving forward, the council will: Continue to fund and support the Refugee Housing Team to help refugees leaving asylum accommodation access private rented housing. Aim to sustain the positive outcomes achieved by Accommodation for Ex-Offenders (AfEO) team within the Home Options team beyond April 2026 when AfEO central government funding ends. Maintain the assisted applicants list and carry out regular outreach to ensure vulnerable residents receive appropriate support. How will the impact of your proposal and actions be measured moving forward? Review of allocation policy impact 1 year from implementation (February 2027) Negative outcomes action plan: Actions identified from EqIA Target completion date (dd/mm/yy) Responsible Officer (role) Comments Action complete Continue and resource Refugee Housing Team Private Rental Sector grants to house refugees leaving asylum accommodation. Ongoing Home Options Manager ☐ Aim to sustain the positive outcomes achieved by Accommodation for Ex-Offenders (AfEO) team within the Home Options team beyond April 2026 when AfEO central government funding ends. 01/04/2026 Home Options Manager ☐ Maintain assisted applicants list and regular outreach to vulnerable applicants. Ongoing Home Options Manager ☐ For the assessment to be final, the relevant people agreeing it must sign it off below. Officer completing assessment Date 04/11/2025 Senior leadership team sponsor Date 05/11/2025 Equality lead (strategy team) Date 04/11/2025 Accessibility: for further information about alternative formats and/or help completing this form, please email strategy@norwich.gov.uk; template revised April 20252

Revisions to the Home Options Policy (561Kb) 5 Housing Development at Mile Cross Depot Site - to follow 6 Nutrient Neutrality Review Scope Purpose - In May 2025, Audit Committee resolved to 'request that Scrutiny Committee considers reviewing the current position around Nutrient Neutrality and the mitigations'. At the June work programming session, the Scrutiny Committee added Nutrient Neutrality to their Work Programme for March 2026. The purpose of this item is for the Scrutiny Committee to scope the review.
